Learning Objectives
Assess muscular deforming forces and injuries associated with femoral shaft fractures.
Specify initial emergency department management and physiologic markers to determine the
timing of surgical management (early appropriate care).
Summarize various femoral shaft treatment options and review the advantages and
disadvantages of each approach.
Determine common complications of the management of femoral shaft fractures and review
how to prevent and manage them.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

Femoral shaft fractures are common injuries that typically result from a high-energy
mechanism of injury.
Management over the past 50 years has substantially evolved so that predictably high union
rates and early functional recovery can be expected with reamed, statically locked
intramedullary nails.
Numerous aspects of femoral shaft fracture management cannot be overlooked, such as
Advanced Trauma Life Support assessment; frequently associated injuries (ipsilateral femoral
neck fracture and ligamentous knee injury); and acceptable fracture length, alignment, and
rotation restoration.
Epidemiology
Annual incidence of 10 to 37 per 100,000 person years
Bimodal age distribution
Young men typically via higher energy mechanism of injury
Older women generally via lower energy mechanism of injury
Epidemiology
A Swedish National Hospital Discharge Registry study found that the median age of males with a
femoral shaft fracture was 27 years compared and the median age of females with a femoral
shaft fracture was 79 years.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Anatomy (Figure 1)
The bony anatomy of the femoral shaft includes an anterior bow.
Compartments of the thigh
Anterior compartment contains the quadriceps muscles and the femoral nerve
Posterior compartment contains the hamstring muscles and the sciatic nerve
Adductor compartment contains the adductor muscles and the obturator nerve
Deforming forces
The abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) insert on the greater trochanter and abduct
the proximal segment.
The iliopsoas inserts on the lesser trochanter and flexes the proximal fragment.
The adductor longus, adductor brevis, gracilis, and adductor magnus have a broad area of
insertion on the distal femur and contribute to a varus force on the distal segment.

Figure 1 Illustrations of the anterior (A) and posterior (B) aspects of the femur show the
origins and insertions of the potential femoral deforming muscular forces. Illustrations also
show the primary muscular attachments on the anterior (A) and posterior (B) aspects of the
femur. (Adapted with permission from Nork SE: Fractures of the shaft of the femur, in Bucholz
RW, Heckman JD, Court-Brown C, eds: Rockwood and Green’s Fractures in Adults, ed 6.
Philadelphia, PA, Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, 2001, p 1852.)

Anatomy and Biomechanics
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
3/48

The anterior femoral bow is commonly quantified as the radius of a circle created by
extending the curved line matching the bow. A cadaver model study of 892 femurs
reported the mean femoral anterior radius of curvature to be 1.2 m.2 Appreciating that
the femoral anterior radius of curvature may be considerably smaller (eg, greater
anterior bow) in particular ethnic groups and in shorter individuals is important to
consider preoperatively. This ensures that the intramedullary nail or the implant with the
most closely matched curvature is considered. For antegrade trochanteric
intramedullary nailing in patients with a decreased femoral anterior radius of curvature,
avoiding a too posterior starting point is essential so that distal anterior cortical
disruption is avoided.
Understanding the muscular deforming forces and their attachment sites on the femur
may help predict the expected fracture deformity and reduction maneuvers necessary
for correction. Muscle paralysis during surgical stabilization aids in minimizing the
muscular deforming forces and allows for easier reduction.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Typical femoral shaft fractures often result from high-energy injuries, such as those sustained
during a motor vehicle collision or a motorcycle accident. The most common mechanism of
injury in motor vehicle collisions is impact of the knee against the car dashboard.
A small percentage of fractures result from repeated stress, such as that experienced by a
young military recruit or a runner after an increase in the intensity of physical training.
Pathologic fractures may be the first presentation of metastatic cancer. Radiographs should be
obtained to evaluate for bony lesions, particularly if the injury is not consistent with the
mechanism of injury.
A fall from a standing height is a common mechanism of injury in elderly patients,
underscoring the need for osteoporotic fracture prevention.
Atypical femoral fractures may occur in the femur from the lesser trochanter to the
supracondylar flare and result from relatively low mechanisms of injury. This fracture typically
occurs in patient with a history of prolonged (>5 years) diphosphonate use.
Historically, bilateral femur fractures were associated with a mortality rate as high as 26%3 A
recent study reported lower death rates (7%).4

Associated Injuries
Pelvis/acetabulum fractures
Hip dislocation
Femoral neck fracture
Ligamentous knee injuries
Fractures of the patella and tibial plateau

Associated Injuries
The two most common associated injuries in patients with a femoral shaft fracture are
ipsilateral femoral neck fracture and ligamentous knee injury. Ipsilateral femoral neck
fracture (Figure 2) occurs in approximately 2% to 9% of all patients with a femoral shaft
fracture but often are missed (in as many as 50% of patients). Initially, these fractures
typically are nondisplaced in as many as 60% of patients. The femoral neck fracture
often is basicervical and vertically oriented.5 Dedicated imaging studies of the femoral
neck are imperative to avoid missing this potentially devastating injury.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
5/48

Figure 2 AP (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the hip demonstrate a midshaft femur
fracture and an ipsilateral femoral neck fracture. (Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD,
Burlington, VT.)
Ligamentous knee injuries commonly occur in patients with a femoral shaft fracture.
Dickson et al6 obtained 27 postoperative knee MRIs to evaluate the extent of soft-tissue

9/3/26, 4:08 PM

injury. The authors reported that anterior cruciate ligament and posterior cruciate
ligament injuries (19% and 7%, respectively) and complete medial collateral ligament and
lateral collateral ligament injuries (19% and 15%, respectively) were common. Most of
the ligamentous injuries were initially diagnosed via physical examination at the
conclusion of femoral shaft fracture surgical management, which highlights the
importance of performing a knee examination in every patient while still sedated after
stabilizing the femoral shaft fracture.
Fracture Classification
The Winquist and Hansen classification system is based on the amount of comminution and
has implications with regard to the use of interlocking screws and postoperative weight-
bearing status (Figure 3).
Figure 3 Illustrations show the Winquist and Hansen classification of femoral shaft fractures.
Type 0, no comminution; type I, minimal or no comminution; type II, at least 50% of the
cortices intact; type III, comminution of at least 50% to 100% of the circumference of the bone;
type IV, no cortical contact at the fracture site with circumferential comminution. (Reproduced

Ridge, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 1990, pp 513- 527.)
The Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification is the internationally
accepted fracture classification system (Figure 4).

distal femur, in Lieberman JR, ed: Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1022-1034.)

Fracture Classification
The Winquist and Hansen classification had greater utility if statically locked
intramedullary nailing was not routinely performed. Fractures with less comminution
and greater cortical contact (types 0, I, and II) would more often not be fully locked, and
patients were more likely allowed to fully bear weight postoperatively compared with
patients with a higher type comminuted fracture. The current standard of care is to use
fully locked intramedullary nails and allow full–weight bearing postoperatively regardless
of the degree of femoral shaft fracture comminution and cortical contact.
The Orthopaedic Trauma Association/AO Foundation classification is an alphanumeric
system that assigns numbers and letters based on the characteristics of the fracture and
its location. The femur is designated the number 3, which is subdivided into three
regions with the number 2 denoting the shaft segment. Therefore, femoral shaft
fractures are categorized as 32, with further delineation based on the pattern and
geometry of the fracture.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Advanced Trauma Life Support principles should be initiated in patients with a femoral shaft
fracture.
Patient History
The mechanism of injury and the details surrounding the injury event should be ascertained, if
possible.
All areas causing the patient pain must be documented and evaluated.
Any prior extremity injuries and pre-injury functional status should be recorded.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
10/48

Obvious thigh deformity with the limb shortened, rotated, and swollen compared with the
contralateral extremity is a common presentation.
The skin should be examined for lacerations and open wounds.
The entire limb should be palpated and inspected.
The presence of pain on palpation, ecchymosis, crepitus, and/or deformity indicates that the
patient should be examined for additional injuries.
The distal extremity must be evaluated for neurovascular integrity.
Sensation in the superficial peroneal, deep peroneal, saphenous, sural and tibial
distributions should be documented.
The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries also should be assessed.
A tertiary examination should be performed after femoral shaft stabilization to ensure no
distracting injuries, such as hand or foot fractures, are overlooked.

Physical Examination
Initial management of patients with a femoral shaft fracture must progress from
preserving life, limb, and limb function, in that order. Advanced Trauma Life Support
protocol can identify any immediately life-threatening situations. Acute limb loss is
uncommon in patients with an isolated femoral shaft fracture; however, vascular injury
and compartment syndrome must be ruled out in every patient. Vascular injury
commonly involves the superficial femoral artery and has been reported to occur in
approximately 1.3% of patients with a closed femoral shaft fracture.7
Imaging Studies
Radiography
An AP view of the pelvis and AP and lateral views of the femur (Figure 5), including the hip and
knee joints, are indicated.

(A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the hip and knee joints demonstrate a femoral shaft fracture.
(Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD, Burlington, VT.)
Computed Tomography
Abdominal/pelvic trauma CT may be used to evaluate the hip to detect an associated
nondisplaced femoral neck fracture after blunt trauma.
Dedicated CT of the left hip without contrast should be considered preoperatively in patients
with an isolated femoral shaft fracture who do not undergo abdominal/pelvic trauma CT.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
A limited role for MRI exists in patients with an acute femoral shaft fracture; however, MRI can
be considered in select patients in whom knee ligamentous or meniscal injury is suspected
and as to detect occult ipsilateral femoral neck fracture ( Figure 6).
Figure 6 Images of the hip of a patient with a femoral shaft fracture. AP (A) and lateral (B)
radiographs demonstrate a femoral shaft fracture. C, Coronal CT scan shows no obvious
femoral neck involvement. Coronal T1-weighted (D) and T2-weighted (E) MRIs show increased
signal intensity in the cranial portion of the femoral neck (arrows), which is consistent with an
occult fracture. (Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD, Burlington, VT.)

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Orthogonal radiographs (AP and lateral views) must be obtained in all patients with a
femoral shaft fracture to fully evaluate the characteristics of the fracture and any
associated injuries; however, controversy exists regarding the appropriate diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
13/48

of ipsilateral femoral neck. Preoperative hip CT with 2-mm slice thickness or less
should be considered in all patients.
Management
Early stabilization of femur fractures (within the first 24 hours postinjury) minimizes
complication rates and may reduce hospital length of stay. Stabilization may consist of initial
skeletal traction, external fixation, or definitive management with an intramedullary nail or
plate.
Skeletal traction is a reasonable early treatment option before definitive skeletal stabilization.
Technique: a centrally threaded Shanz pin or a tensioned Kirschner wire
Location: distal femur or proximal tibia

Management
Temporary stabilization of all femoral shaft fractures is highly recommended. A study by
Bumpass et al8 compared patients with a femoral shaft fracture who underwent initial
stabilization via a long leg splint versus distal femoral skeletal traction. The authors
reported no differences between the groups at 6 months postinjury based on Lysholm
Knee Scale scores, indicating minimal knee function complications from a distal femoral
traction pin. In addition, the skeletal traction group had substantially less pain during
immobilization application. Even et al9 reported that preoperative cutaneous traction (ie,
Buck traction) is as effective as skeletal traction with regard to preoperative pain
improvement; however, all the patients in this study were definitively treated within 24
hours postinjury. Therefore, skeletal traction should be used in patients with frail skin or
those in whom surgical management is delayed.
Nonsurgical Management
Limited indications
Traction management becoming lost skill

Techniques/Procedures
Centrally threaded pin or tensioned wire placed in the distal femur or the proximal tibia
(Figure 7)
Various traction systems exist (eg, Russell, Perkins, etc.), with different attachments or bed
modifications that can be used to manipulate the proximal and distal fracture segments and
allow knee motion.
Total time in traction may range from 4 to 12 weeks
Figure 7 Knee radiographs demonstrate various skeletal traction options. AP (A) and lateral
(B) radiographs demonstrate a distal femoral centrally threaded pin. AP (C) and lateral (D)
radiographs demonstrate a tensioned distal femur wire. AP (E) and lateral (F) radiographs
demonstrate a centrally threaded proximal tibial pin. A tensioned wire in the proximal tibia
also can be used. (Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD, Burlington, VT.)
Outcomes
Long periods of bed rest may be detrimental, and patients should be monitored closely.
Patients should be evaluated for pin tract infection and decubiti secondary to prolonged
immobilization.
Serial radiographs should be obtained to monitor for distraction at the fracture site during
management.
Mechanical and chemical deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis should be instituted.
Malunion, knee stiffness and pin site infection are common complications.

Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
15/48

Nonsurgical management of femoral shaft fractures consisting of sustained skeletal
traction is rare in areas where intramedullary nails are readily available. Nonsurgical
management is associated with high union rates, albeit delayed and commonly
malunited, and avoidance of surgical complications, such as deep infection or implant-
related pain; however, other complications, such as knee stiffness and pin site infections,
are common after nonsurgical management. The Perkins traction method allows for
knee motion to occur if tolerated by the patient, using a split bed that folds away at the
knee. One series of patients in whom the Perkins traction method was used reported
that 94% of patients had clinical and radiographic union by 12 weeks, with 66% of
patients having no limb-length discrepancy and 60% of patients having full knee range of
motion.10
Surgical Management
A reamed, statically locked intramedullary nail is the standard of care for femoral shaft
fractures.
Central placement of an intramedullary nail within the femoral canal results in lower tensile
and shear stresses on the implant compared with plate fixation.
Intramedullary nailing is associated with several benefits over plates and screws, including
less extensive exposure and dissection, a lower infection rate, less quadriceps scarring,
earlier functional use of the extremity, immediate full–weight bearing, rapid fracture healing,
and a low refracture rate.
The nail starting point should be based on surgeon preference.
Antegrade
Piriformis entry
Trochanteric entry
Retrograde
At least two interlocking screws, one proximal and one distal, should be used for all
fractures.
For femoral fractures with segmental comminution, multiple interlocking screws proximally
and distally should be considered.
Retrograde approach
Relative indications for this approach include multiple-system trauma; trauma to the
ipsilateral extremity, pelvis/acetabulum, and/or spine; bilateral femur fractures; morbid
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
16/48

obesity; and pregnancy.
The overall union rate associated with retrograde nailing is comparable with that of
antegrade nailing.
The approach is associated with several advantages, including ease of entry point, potentially
shorter surgical times, and avoidance of a fracture table.
The recommended starting point for retrograde nailing in the coronal plane is in line with the
femoral canal, which typically is at the medial margin of the intercondylar notch (Figure 8, A).
The optimal starting point in the sagittal plane is approximately 10 mm anterior to the
posterior cruciate ligament, which radiographically corresponds with just anterior to the
Blumensaat line (Figure 8, B). The Blumensaat line can be visualized on lateral radiographs.
The line represents the intercondylar notch roof.
Figure 8 AP (A) and lateral (B) fluoroscopic images of a knee show the starting point for a retrograde
intramedullary nail. (Panel A courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD, Burlington, VT; panel B reproduced from
Gage MJ, Yoon RS: Fractures of the femoral shaft and distal femur, in Lieberman JR, ed: Comprehensive

Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2020, pp 1022-
1034.) 
Complications include malrotation and knee pain.
Antegrade: piriformis entry point
This entry point is in line with the mechanical axis of the femur (Figure 9).
An excessively anterior entry point increases the risk for femoral neck fracture secondary to
hoop stresses during nail insertion.
Injury to the blood supply of the femoral head is more likely with a piriformis entry point
rather than a trochanteric entry point; however, no substantial difference in femoral head
perfusion or osteonecrosis rates have been observed in adults.
Using a piriformis entry point minimizes the risk of deformity, specifically varus, in patients
with a proximal femur fracture.
Figure 9 AP (A) and lateral (B) fluoroscopic images of a hip show a piriformis starting point.
Note that the wire is in line with the femoral shaft. (Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD,
Burlington, VT.)
Antegrade: trochanteric entry point
The main advantage over a piriformis entry point is that it is a more accessible starting point
(Figure 10)

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
18/48

Decreased surgical time
Decreased fluoroscopy use
Potential complications include iatrogenic varus malreduction if the nail does not match the
patient’s anatomy
Figure 10 AP (A) and lateral (B) fluoroscopic images of a hip show a greater trochanteric
starting point. (Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD, Burlington, VT.)
Reamed versus unreamed intramedullary nailing
Reamed intramedullary nailing is recommended over unreamed nailing because it is
associated with improved rates of healing and decreased complications.
Previous concerns with reaming included an increased incidence of acute respiratory distress
syndrome (ARDS) and lung complications in patients who had associated pulmonary injury;
however, no substantial difference has been found in pulmonary complications between
reamed and unreamed cohorts.
Fracture table with traction versus supine and lateral free leg positions
The decision to use a fracture table with traction (Figure 11) or a radiolucent flat table
(Figure 12) with the patient in the supine or lateral position must be made for all antegrade
intramedullary nailing procedures.
Considerations include fracture pattern, body habitus, number of assistants available,
associated injuries, and surgeon preference.

Multiple complications have been reported with the use of a fracture table, including
pudendal nerve neurapraxia and compartment syndrome of the unaffected leg. In addition,
positioning a patient with multiple injuries on a fracture table or in a lateral position
occasionally may be contraindicated.
Figure 11 Intraoperative photograph of a patient with a femoral shaft fracture placed in the
supine position on a fracture table. (Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD, Burlington, VT.)
Figure 12 Intraoperative photograph of a patient with a femoral shaft fracture placed in the
supine position on a radiolucent table. (Courtesy of Patrick C. Schottel, MD, Burlington, VT.)
Plate and screw fixation
Plate fixation of femur fractures is not commonly used and has few indications.
Consider femoral plating for the following
Periprosthetic fracture

Interprosthetic/inter-implant fracture
Preexisting femoral deformity that would preclude passage of a nail
Small or obliterated intramedullary canal
Complications of compression plating
Failed fixation
Infection
Nonunion
Devitalization of fracture fragments with excessive periosteal stripping
Stress shielding with possible refracture
External fixation
Most frequently used for temporary skeletal stabilization in damage control orthopaedics.
Unstable and/or underresuscitated polytrauma patient
Open wound gross contamination or soft-tissue compromise that does not permit initial
definitive fracture fixation.
Facilitates greater mobilization and ease of care in critically ill patients compared with
skeletal traction.
Concerns regarding external fixation
Pin tract infection
Timing of temporary external fixation conversion to intramedullary nailing and risk of deep
infection.
Ipsilateral femoral neck and shaft fractures
Radiographic evaluation
Most femoral neck fractures that are associated with an ipsilateral shaft fracture are
vertically oriented and nondisplaced or minimally displaced, making radiographic detection
difficult.
Fine-cut CT scans may help detect most, but not all, femoral neck fractures preoperatively.
Management
The timing of discovery of femoral neck fractures has implications on management.
Regardless when the fracture is discovered, anatomic reduction and optimal femoral neck
fracture stabilization are essential.
One or two devices may be used to manage the associated shaft and neck fractures. With
one device, a cephalomedullary or reconstruction nail may be used. With two devices, a
retrograde nail with cannulated screws or a sliding hip screw is recommended.
Open femoral shaft fractures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
21/48

Open femoral shaft fractures should be managed urgently via irrigation and débridement
and via temporary or definitive fixation, depending on the patient scenario.
An incision should be made that allows for adequate visualization and débridement of both
fractured bone ends and the entire zone of injury.
No increased rate of infection is observed with retrograde nailing compared with antegrade
nailing of open femur fractures; however, retrograde nailing theoretically risks spread of
infection into the knee joint.
The infection rate in patients with an open femur fracture is substantially lower than that in
patients with an open tibia fracture.

Surgical Management
Reamed, statically locked intramedullary femoral nailing is the standard of care for
femoral shaft fractures. Classic studies have reported union rates as high as 98% to
99%.11,12 Initial intramedullary nailing technique assessed the degree of cortical
comminution using the Winquist and Hansen classification system to determine the
degree of cortical bone apposition and fracture length stability to inform the decision to
lock the nail or not. Proximally and distally locked nails were routinely dynamized
secondarily to increase fracture site compression and union; however, subsequent
studies determined that routine dynamization was unnecessary given the high union
rate with statically locked nails and the potential shortening associated with early nail
dynamization.13 Initial intramedullary nails were straight in the coronal plane and had to
be inserted through the piriformis fossa. In the past two decades, advancements in nail
design have allowed for alternative femoral intramedullary nailing starting points that
can be used based on unique patient and fracture characteristics.
Comparative studies have found that retrograde femoral intramedullary nailing results
in union rates equivalent to those of antegrade nailing.14-16 A prospective randomized
trial by Ostrum et al14 compared clinical and radiographic outcomes of 100 femoral shaft
fractures managed via a piriformis starting point antegrade nail or retrograde nail. The
authors reported that antegrade and retrograde nail insertion sites resulted in a high
union rate (100% versus 98%, respectively). Ricci et al16 reported that the incidence of
knee pain was substantially higher after retrograde intramedullary nailing versus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
22/48

antegrade intramedullary nailing (36% versus 9%); however, the antegrade
intramedullary nailing group was 2.5 times more likely to report hip pain compared with
the retrograde intramedullary nailing group.
Retrograde intramedullary nailing for femoral shaft fractures is associated with
advantages and disadvantages compared with antegrade nailing. Each patient’s fracture
characteristics, associated injuries, and comorbidities must be considered in deciding
between retrograde or antegrade nailing.
Antegrade intramedullary nailing using a piriformis entry point is the classic technique
because the initial commercially available antegrade nails were all straight in the coronal
plane. The use of a piriformis entry point has been reported to result in hip abductor
and extensor muscle weakness but without considerable gait or long-term functional
impairment.17
In a cadaver model study of different intramedullary nailing entry points, Dora et al18
reported that anterior branches of the deep medial femoral circumflex artery were
damaged in all specimens with a piriformis starting point. The authors advised against
the use of a piriformis entry point because of terminal medial femoral circumflex artery
branch damage. Another cadaver model study investigating femoral head perfusion
using gadolinium-enhanced MRI reported no decreased perfusion in the piriformis entry
point cohort, even with injury to some terminal deep medial femoral circumflex artery
branches.19
Piriformis entry nailing is especially helpful in patients with a more proximal femoral
shaft fracture, especially atypical fractures. This entry point minimizes the risks of
iatrogenic coronal plane deformity because of mismatch between the trochanteric entry
point and the proximal bend of a trochanteric intramedullary nail.
Numerous studies have compared piriformis and trochanteric entry antegrade
intramedullary nailing. No substantial long-term difference in function or clinical
outcomes have been found between the two entry points;20,21 however, trochanteric
entry intramedullary nails consistently have been found to result in shorter surgical time
and decreased fluoroscopy use.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:08 PM
AAOS | Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001083
23/48

One potential complication with trochanteric entry intramedullary nails is iatrogenic
varus malreduction in proximal femoral shaft and subtrochanteric fracture locations. To
avoid varus malalignment, the trochanteric entry point should be located on the tip or,
preferably, slightly medial to the tip of the greater trochanter.22 A too lateral entry point
should be avoided. Another potential complication is distal anterior cortical disruption.
Modern implants with a smaller radius of curvature are less likely to result in anterior
cortical penetration, especially if an excessively posterior starting point is avoided.
The initial intramedullary nailing technique introduced by Küntscher advocated for
reaming to larger diameter unlocked nails that would result in a more secure cortical fit;
however, the development of locking nails and concerns regarding the physiologic and
pulmonary effects of reaming resulted in questions regarding the necessity of this
technique. This led to numerous studies comparing reamed versus unreamed femoral
intramedullary nails.23-25 These studies reported that reaming was not inferior to
unreamed nails and resulted in fewer complications and faster time to union; however, it
was associated with longer surgical times and greater intraoperative blood loss.
In a recent retrospective study of 484 femoral shaft fractures, Serrano et al26
investigated the effect of reaming and the ability to implant larger diameter nails.
Specifically, the authors studied whether the degree of overreaming (<1 mm, 1 to 2 mm
or >2 mm) and the size of the implanted nail had any effect on union rate. The authors
reported that increased overreaming and larger nail size were not associated with a
substantially higher union rate. Therefore, a standard femoral intramedullary nail size of
10 mm with overreaming by 1 to 1.5 mm or less is acceptable. Larger nail sizes should be
used for metadiaphyseal locations and certain midshaft fracture patterns to improve
alignment if necessary.
A survey of orthopaedic trauma surgeons summarizing their preferred positioning for
isolated femoral shaft fracture management was recently published by Rubinger et al.27
The authors reported that most of the 171 respondents preferred a fracture table with
traction (95 of 171; 56%) compared with supine (49 of 171; 29%) or direct lateral (21 of
171; 12%) free leg positioning. A prospective study reported that supine free leg nailing
reduced surgical time and rotational malreduction compared with the fracture table but
ultimately resulted in no difference in postoperative functional outcomes.28 Preferably,

Plate fixation of native femoral shaft fractures is less common than nailing given the high
union rate and low complication rate associated with reamed, statically locked
intramedullary nailing. In general, plate fixation also necessitates a more prolonged
period of protected–weight bearing than intramedullary nailing; however, particular
clinical scenarios, such as periprosthetic fracture, femoral deformity, small or obliterated
intramedullary canal, and interprosthetic/inter-implant fractures, necessitate
consideration of plate fixation. Plating usually involves the use of a broad, large fragment
plate (Figure 13). The fracture pattern and location will dictate whether direct reduction
with absolute stability plating or indirect reduction and relative stability plating is
performed.

Conversion to definitive fixation typically occurs after the patient is physiologically stable
enough to proceed with surgical management, which is determined via different
parameters. High union rates and low infection rates can be expected;29 however,
conversion should occur within 14 days to minimize the risk of pin site contamination
and possible infection.30
An ipsilateral femoral neck fracture is an important associated injury that must not be
missed (Resource 1). Most ipsilateral femoral neck fractures are nondisplaced, and
advanced imaging studies typically are recommended. Tornetta et al31 reported the
effectiveness of implementing a protocol for evaluating the femoral neck in all patients
with a femoral shaft fracture. The authors obtained a dedicated internal rotation AP
femoral neck radiograph and a CT scan without contrast using 2-mm slice thickness
preoperatively. In addition, the authors performed intraoperative fluoroscopy of the
femoral neck and obtained dedicated radiographs at the conclusion of femoral shaft
fixation. Using this protocol, the authors reported a 91% reduction in delayed diagnosis
of associated femoral neck fractures.
Other studies have questioned the effectiveness of preoperative CT in identifying
ipsilateral femoral neck fractures. Cannada et al32 reviewed a cohort of patients with a
femoral shaft fracture from the Southeastern Fracture Consortium. The authors
reported that, of the patients with a combined femoral neck-shaft fracture, 67 patients
had undergone a preoperative CT scan. Of these patients, no evidence of a femoral neck
fracture was observed on the CT scans of 12 patients (18%). In addition, O’Toole et al33
performed a blinded imaging comparison between patients who had a femoral shaft
fracture with or without an ipsilateral femoral neck fracture. Five fellowship-trained
orthopaedic surgeons reviewed the preoperative radiographs and CT scans of the
patients. The authors reported that the preoperative imaging studies were associated
with a consistently low sensitivity (56% to 64%) between the different surgeon raters.
Regardless whether preoperative CT is performed, surgeons must maintain a high index
of suspicion and not miss ipsilateral femoral neck fractures by scrutinizing all
preoperative, intraoperative, and immediately postoperative imaging studies. A recent
study reported that rapid, limited-sequence MRI was effective in diagnosing associated
femoral neck fractures in patients with a negative CT scan.34 The most cost-effective and


Nonunion
Femoral shaft nonunions are uncommon. Numerous techniques, such as nail
dynamization, reamed exchange nailing, and augmentative plating with bone grafting,
are available to manage nonunions. The most common procedure is reamed exchange
nailing, which is associated with a success rate of approximately 80%.38,39 Ideally,
reamed exchange nailing should aim to implant a new intramedullary nail that is 2 mm
or larger in diameter. Alternatively, augmentative plating and bone grafting also has
been found to result in a high union rate. This technique has been reported to be better
than reamed exchange nailing in patients with a non-isthmal femoral shaft fracture
nonunion.40,41 Regardless of the surgical technique used, a nonunion workup consisting
of inflammatory and metabolic serum markers should be considered in all patients.
Malunion
Malunion may manifest as a discrepancy in femoral length, alignment, and/or rotation
compared with the contralateral uninjured femur.
Limb-length discrepancies less than 20 mm typically can be managed nonsurgically with the
use of shoe lifts or shoe modifications.
Rotational limb deformities are not uncommon and are estimated to occur in as many as 20%
of patients.
Typically, rotational deformities of less than 15° are well tolerated.


severity of clinical manifestations of malrotation may be unpredictable because of

femoral intramedullary nailing on a fracture table with traction compared with free leg
positioning.28
Venous Thromboembolism
Venous thromboembolism is a concern in trauma patients, especially those with long bone
trauma, pelvic and acetabular fractures, and spine trauma. It may lead to a fatal pulmonary
embolism.
Duplex ultrasonography may be used to diagnose deep vein thrombosis if clinically suspected.
The symptoms of a pulmonary embolism include acute-onset tachypnea, tachycardia, low-
grade fever, hypoxia, mental status changes, and chest pain.
In patients in whom a pulmonary embolism is suspected, CT with contrast, ventilation-
perfusion scanning, or pulmonary angiography may be used for diagnosis.
Preventive measures include chemical prophylaxis (low-molecular-weight heparin is
preferred), sequential compression devices, and early surgical stabilization with subsequent
mobilization.

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Nerve palsy
In femur fractures stabilized on a fracture table, pudendal nerve palsy may result from
excessive traction and/or improper positioning with the perineal post.
Peroneal nerve neurapraxia may occur secondary to excessive traction or direct compression
in the uninjured leg with the improper use of a well leg holder.
Appropriate padding and expeditious surgical management can mitigate this complication.
Other Complications
Fat embolism syndrome
This usually occurs 24 to 72 hours postinjury in a small percentage of patients with a long
bone fracture.
It may be fatal in as many as 15% of patients.
Diagnosis is based on the presence of at least one major criterion and four minor criteria.
Major criteria: hypoxemia, altered mental status, petechial rash, pulmonary edema
Minor criteria: tachycardia, pyrexia, retinal emboli, fat in urine/sputum, thrombocytopenia,
anemia
Management includes mechanical ventilation with high positive end-expiratory pressure
levels.
Prevention involves early (within 24 hours) stabilization of long bone fractures.
ARDS
ARDS is acute respiratory failure with pulmonary edema.
It may result from multiple etiologies and is known to occur after trauma and shock.
The patient may be difficult to ventilate secondary to decreased lung compliance.

Other signs and symptoms include tachypnea, tachycardia, and hypoxemia.
Management consists of high positive end-expiratory pressure.
The mortality rate may be as high as 50%.
Early appropriate stabilization of long bone fractures minimizes ongoing soft-tissue injury
and helps reduce the incidence of ARDS.
Compartment syndrome
Compartment syndrome of the thigh is rare after femur fracture. Concomitant vascular
injury must be ruled out, and the mechanism of injury must be considered.
A crush injury or an injury involving a prolonged extrication should be followed closely.
Compartment syndrome has been reported in the uninjured extremity after intramedullary
nailing on a fracture table with the use of a well leg holder.
Heterotopic ossification
The insertion site for an antegrade nail involves disruption of the abductor muscles.
Therefore, heterotopic ossification about the hip may occur in some patients.
Heterotopic ossification of minimal clinical importance has been reported to occur in as
many as 26% of patients with a fracture stabilized via a piriformis starting point. The
occurrence rate associated with a trochanteric starting point has not yet been reported.

Other Complications
The timing of definitive femoral shaft fixation is critically important. Inadequate
resuscitation and early complete surgical management may result in ARDS and an
increased mortality risk. Earlier approaches to polytrauma patients with a femoral shaft
fracture thought that early total care was the best option to stabilize soft-tissue injury
and improve mobilization. Because of concerns that early total care was resulting in
unacceptably high rates of ARDS, a subsequent push for more initial temporary
measures followed by delayed definitive fixation occurred. This damage control
orthopaedics approach minimized the risk of a second hit to patients but also delayed
definitive management. A new approach termed early appropriate care uses physiologic
markers to recognize patients who are adequately resuscitated and clinically stable
enough for definitive treatment. Physiologic markers, such as a pH level greater than or
equal to 7.25, a lactate level less than 4.0 mmol/L, and a base excess level greater than
or equal to -5.5 mmol/L, have been reported.47 A study specifically assessing the timing

Unique Femoral Shaft Fracture Patterns
Atypical femur fractures
With prolonged use of diphosphonates, bone turnover rate decreases considerably. These
are hypothesized to be insufficiency fractures that resulted from severely suppressed bone
turnover and the accumulation of skeletal microdamage.
Patients typically sustain these fractures from a low-energy mechanism of injury (eg, giving
way at standing height).
These fractures have a characteristic pattern.
They tend to be simple transverse or oblique fractures.
Cortical thickening occurs around the fracture site (Figure 16).
Lateral or medial beaking occurs.
The medial cortex of the distal segment tends to have a proximally oriented fracture line.

Interprosthetic/inter-implant fractures of the femoral shaft
An interprosthetic fracture is a fracture between a hip prosthesis and a knee prosthesis
(Figure 17).
Inter-implant fractures can occur between a short hip nail and a knee prosthesis.
The incidence is increasing.
Most often, affected patients already have compromised bone quality, which must be
considered in creating treatment plans.
Plate fixation is the preferred treatment option. Intramedullary retrograde nailing in patients
with poor bone quality who have a cruciate-retaining or open-box, posterior-stabilized knee
arthroplasty implant can supplement fixation. Fixation should extend proximal to the distal
extent of the hip implant and span most of the femur to avoid stress risers.

Interprosthetic/inter-implant fractures are becoming more common. Assessment of the
fracture location and the stability of the hip and knee prosthesis is critical. If the
prosthesis is unstable, then consideration of a revision prosthesis is strongly
encouraged. Typically, interprosthetic/inter-implant fractures are managed via lateral
locking plate fixation. Supplementing fixation with tensioned cerclage cables also can be
performed. Adding a femoral cortical strut allograft to a lateral locking plate construct is
an additional treatment option that has been shown to result in higher failure loads if
placed medially but at an unknown biologic cost because of the need for greater fracture
site exposure.52 In patients with a knee prosthesis that has no box (cruciate-retaining) or
an open box (posterior-stabilized) design, a retrograde intramedullary nail can be used
in addition to the spanning lateral locking plate to supplement fixation. Lateral locked
plating should sufficiently span both prostheses as much as possible to prevent future
peri-implant fracture.

Rehabilitation
With stable fracture fixation, early mobilization and weight bearing are permitted. Most
patients who undergo intramedullary nail fixation are permitted to bear weight as tolerated;
however, associated injuries, implant selection, and surgeon preference dictate exact
postoperative rehabilitation protocols.
Early active motion of the hip and knee joint is encouraged.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Examine all patients to rule out rare complications, such as vascular injury and compartment
syndrome.
Assess the patient preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively for associated injuries,
such as an ipsilateral femoral neck fracture and ligamentous knee injury.
Early fracture stabilization via skeletal traction, external fixation, or definitive fixation with an
intramedullary nail or plate within 24 hours postinjury is encouraged.
The timing of definitive fixation is based on physiologic markers to minimize the complications
of a second hit in underresuscitated patients.
A reamed, statically locked intramedullary nail is the preferred treatment option for most
femoral shaft fractures. The decision of whether to use a retrograde or antegrade approach, a
piriformis or trochanteric entry point, or a fracture table or a free leg supine or lateral position
is based on surgeon preference and other associated injuries.
